findings.title: `ttIs(t, "void")` can never be true (`void` is TY_VOID, not TY_BUILTIN): a bare `return` inside any `-> void` function and every void-returning lambda are rejected, while the `new void` guards it also disables stay dead
findings.why: `void` is interned as `mkType(a, TY_VOID, "void")` (types.c:70) and `"void"` is not in BUILTIN_NAMES (types.c:18-24), so `ttIs(x, "void")` requires `x->kind == TY_BUILTIN`, which no void-typed value ever has -- the predicate is unconditionally false for the one name six call sites use it with. (a) check_stmt.c:1031 `if (want && !ttIs(want, "void"))` is the guard that lets a bare `return` pass in a value-less function; it never fires, so a `return` inside a `-> void` function is reported as '`g` must return a value of type `void`' -- a self-contradictory diagnostic and a false rejection of the ordinary guard-clause idiom. (b) check_expr.c:919 `if (cf->ret && !ttIs(cf->ret, "void") && !w.sawReturn)` is the lambda counterpart: a lambda declared `-> void` with an empty body is rejected, and writing `{ return }` in it instead hits the same check_stmt.c:1031 guard ('`call` must return a value of type `void`'), so a void-returning lambda has no writable form at all. (c) check_expr.c:2289 `else if (ttIs(w, "void") || ttIsError(w))` and check_top.c:4856 `if (nt->kind == TY_PARAM || ttHasParam(nt) || ttIs(nt, "void"))` are the two guards that exist to reject `new void`; both are dead, so `new void` and `new T` with T instantiated to void compile and emit `(int64_t)sizeof(void)` (a GNU extension; 1 byte). check_top.c:80 (`if (f->ret && ttIs(f->ret, "void")) f->ret = NULL;`) is dead for the same reason, which is why the lambda's `call` keeps `tVoid` instead of NULL and trips (b).
findings.trigger: Any function declared `-> void` that contains a `return` statement; any lambda declared `-> void`; `new void` or a generic `new T` instantiated with `T = void`.
findings.repro:
cd /tmp/tt
# t_vret.extc: fn g() -> void { return }
/home/alphayang/extC_Compiler/build/extc -w t_vret.extc -o /dev/null
-> t_vret.extc:1:1: error: `g` must return a value of type `void`
# t_vret3.extc: fn g() { return }  (no declared return type) -> rc=0, i.e. the trigger is exactly the ttIs(...,"void") test
/home/alphayang/extC_Compiler/build/extc -w t_vret3.extc -o /dev/null   # rc=0
# t_lam.extc: var f = fn(x: i32) -> void { }   /  t_lam2.extc: fn() -> void { return }
/home/alphayang/extC_Compiler/build/extc -w t_lam.extc  -o /dev/null
-> error: this lambda returns no value, but its type says `void`
/home/alphayang/extC_Compiler/build/extc -w t_lam2.extc -o /dev/null
-> error: `call` must return a value of type `void`
# t_newvoid.extc: var p: mut ref void = new void
/home/alphayang/extC_Compiler/build/extc -w t_newvoid.extc -o t_newvoid.c   # rc=0
grep -n 'sizeof(void)' t_newvoid.c   # -> extc_arena_alloc(..., (int64_t)sizeof(void), ...)
# t_mkv.extc: fn mkone<T>() -> mut ref T { return new T }  +  mkone<void>()  -> rc=0 (deferred guard also dead)

findings.title: The generated C name of an array type (`array_<len>_<elem>`) and of a generic-enum instance (`<enum>_<arg>`) is not reserved: a user declaration with that name yields two `struct` definitions for one tag, and extc still exits 0
findings.why: ttMangle gives a fixed array the C name `array_<n>_<elem>` (types.c:483-485); ttEnumGeneric gives a generic enum instance `<edef>_<arg>...` (types.c:708-715). Neither namespace is reserved against user declarations. codegen.c:6696-6718 is a guard written for exactly this failure ('two definitions of `struct pair_i64` -- gcc refused the whole file', tools/attack.py A5), but its loop body starts with `if (!inst || inst->kind != TY_GENERIC || !inst->sdef || !inst->name) continue;` (codegen.c:6698): the TY_ARRAY entries that live in the same `tt->instances` vector (pushed at types.c:140) are skipped, and generic enum instances are not in that vector at all (tt->enumInstances, types.c:717). Consequently `struct array_3_i32` written by the user and `[3]i32` emit two `struct array_3_i32` definitions; the compiler reports success and the artifact does not compile.
findings.trigger: A program that declares a struct whose name equals the mangled C name of a type it uses: `struct array_3_i32 { x: i32 }` together with any `[3]i32`, or `struct option_i32 { x: i32 }` together with any `option<i32>`.
findings.repro:
cd /tmp/tt
# t_arr.extc: struct array_3_i32 { x: i32 }  +  var a: [3]i32 = [1, 2, 3]
/home/alphayang/extC_Compiler/build/extc -w t_arr.extc -o t_arr.c ; echo rc=$?   # rc=0
gcc -fsyntax-only -w t_arr.c
-> t_arr.c:117:1: error: redefinition of struct or union 'struct array_3_i32' (first at t_arr.c:83)
# t_enum.extc: struct option_i32 { x: i32 }  +  var o: option<i32> = option<i32>::some(5)
/home/alphayang/extC_Compiler/build/extc -w t_enum.extc -o t_enum.c ; echo rc=$?  # rc=0
gcc -fsyntax-only -w t_enum.c
-> t_enum.c:107:1: error: redefinition of struct or union 'struct option_i32'
# --check-c does catch it (rc=1, 'extc: **the generated C does not compile** -- this is an extc bug'), so only the default path is broken

findings.title: `mut` is silently discarded for every non-generic name (`mut i32`, `mut point`) and for generic enum instances (`mut option<i32>`), although the same modifier on a generic struct is a hard error
findings.why: The only place that rules on `t->mut` is inside the `if (t->targs.len > 0)` block for generic structs (types.c:349-362). Two paths bypass it: (a) `t->targs.len == 0` -- a builtin, a non-generic struct, a payload-free enum -- falls through this block to `return base;` (line 379) with `t->mut` never inspected; (b) a generic *enum* instance leaves at line 322 (`return ttEnumGeneric(tt, base->edef, &eargs)`) before the check. The parser deliberately defers the decision ('Whether `slice<T>` really is a view cannot be decided here, because the name is not resolved yet, so this only records the modifier and the type checker rules on it', parser.c:1690-1703), and the checker's own message ('`mut` cannot qualify `%s`', types.c:355-358) states the rule, so the qualifier is silently dropped for exactly the shapes the parser cannot judge. `mut` is a permission in this language ('no code may invent a permission', types.h:266-267), so a permission word that is accepted and then ignored is a silent loss of the author's annotation, not a style issue.
findings.trigger: `mut` written in front of a builtin (a parameter `x: mut i32`), a non-generic struct (`p: mut point`), or a generic enum instance (`o: mut option<i32>`).
findings.repro:
cd /tmp/tt
# t_mut1.extc: fn f(x: mut i32) -> i32
/home/alphayang/extC_Compiler/build/extc -w t_mut1.extc -o /dev/null   # rc=0, no diagnostic at all
# t_mut4.extc: struct point { x: i32 }  fn f(p: mut point) -> i32
/home/alphayang/extC_Compiler/build/extc -w t_mut4.extc -o t_mut4.c   # rc=0, no diagnostic
# t_mut2.extc: fn f(x: mut option<i32>) -> i32
/home/alphayang/extC_Compiler/build/extc -w t_mut2.extc -o /dev/null   # rc=0, no diagnostic
# t_mut3.extc: struct pair<A,B>{...}  fn f(x: mut pair<i32,i32>) -> i32
/home/alphayang/extC_Compiler/build/extc -w t_mut3.extc -o /dev/null
-> error: `mut` cannot qualify `pair`

findings.title: A module's own declaration is unreachable by its bare name when the prelude declares the same name: the plain-name lookup wins over the module alias table, so the module is forced to use the prelude's type
findings.why: The alias table (`unit` -> `lib4$unit`) is what lets a module's renamed declaration be found by the name its source wrote, but it is consulted only when `ttFromName(tt, nm0)` fails (types.c:275). The prelude's declarations are registered into the same table first (main.c:253 `ttRegister(tt, &pm)`), so a module that declares a type with a prelude type's name gets the *prelude's* type from the bare name and its own declaration is never considered. Only the root file is protected by the reserved-definition check (check_top.c:97-110), and that check compares names *after* module declarations have already been renamed to `lib$Name`, so a module may legally declare `struct unit` and then be unable to use it: the annotation is rewritten to the module's own `lib4$unit` while the literal's name string is not, so one self-consistent module is rejected with a diagnostic that names a type the author never mixed up ('expects `lib4::unit`, found `unit`'). With a prelude struct that has the same field names the two types would be interchangeable silently, which is the outcome the alias logic exists to prevent ('the worst outcome', types.c:278-281).
findings.trigger: A file loaded as a module (`use lib4`) declares a struct/enum whose name the prelude also declares (`unit`, `coroutine`, `option`, `result`, `pcg32`, `varArray`, `slice`, `domain`) and then names it in expression position -- a struct literal `unit { ... }`, `Name<args>::f(...)`, or a variant path.
findings.repro:
cd /tmp/tt
# lib4.extc: struct unit { n: i32 }  fn mk() -> unit { return unit { } }
# m4.extc:    use lib4   fn main() -> i32 { var u: lib4::unit = lib4::mk()  return 1 }
/home/alphayang/extC_Compiler/build/extc -w m4.extc -o m4.c
-> ./lib4.extc:3:1: error: return value expects `lib4::unit`, found `unit`
# m1.extc/lib1.extc variant (return unit { n: 7 }):
-> ./lib1.extc:4:1: error: struct `unit` has no field `n`   note: fields of unit:   (the prelude's empty struct)

findings.title: A type parameter written with type arguments (`T<i32>`) silently resolves to `T`: the arguments are dropped instead of rejected
findings.why: The type-parameter branch of ttResolve returns as soon as the written name matches a parameter in scope and never looks at `t->targs`, so `T<i32>` is accepted and treated as `T`. Every other name path rejects a wrong argument count ('`pair` expects 2 type argument(s), got 1', types.c:312-314), and the same file's `ttArray`/generic paths are careful about arity; here the written arguments are silently discarded, which is the class of 'accepted but not what was written' binding the file's own comments call worse than a rejection (types.c:250-256).
findings.trigger: A generic declaration that writes type arguments on one of its own type parameters, e.g. `fn f<T>(x: T<i32>) -> i32`.
findings.repro:
cd /tmp/tt
# t_targ2.extc: fn f<T>(x: T<i32>) -> i32 { return 0 }  +  f<i32>(y)
/home/alphayang/extC_Compiler/build/extc -w t_targ2.extc -o t_targ2.c ; echo rc=$?   # rc=0
grep -n 'f_i32' t_targ2.c   # -> static int32_t f_i32(int32_t x);   (the <i32> on T vanished)
# control (same mistake on a real generic is diagnosed):
# t_targ3.extc: var p: pair<i32> = { a: 1, b: 2 }  -> error: `pair` expects 2 type argument(s), got 1

findings.title: The unknown-type diagnostic advertises `str` as a built-in type, but no such type exists
findings.why: The note lists `str` among the built-in types, but BUILTIN_NAMES (types.c:18-24) has no `str`, ttFromName has no other source for it, and neither the prelude nor the stdlib declares a type of that name (grep 'struct str|type str' over stdlib/ finds only `string` in stdlib/stl/string.extc). So the compiler tells the user to write a type that it will itself reject with the very same message -- a self-contradictory diagnostic that sends the reader looking for a missing `use`.
findings.trigger: Any program naming an undefined type (`var s: str = ...`) prints the note.
findings.repro:
cd /tmp/tt
# t_str.extc: fn main() -> i32 { var s: str = 0  return 0 }
/home/alphayang/extC_Compiler/build/extc -w t_str.extc -o /dev/null
-> error: unknown type `str`
   note: built-in types: i8 i16 i32 i64 u8 u16 u32 u64 f32 f64 bool str void
# grep -rn 'struct str\|type str' stdlib/  -> no match (only `struct string` in stdlib/stl/string.extc)

coverage_notes:
Read src/types.c (all 1288 lines) and src/types.h (all 472 lines) in full, plus the callers of every exported function (check_top.c, check_expr.c, check_stmt.c, check.c, check_lookup.c, codegen.c, modules.c, parser.c, main.c) for the invariants each one relies on.

Verified-correct points (checked, not reported): ttCanWiden's lattice (sign-preserving same-width, u->i only when strictly wider, int->float only when bits <= 24/53, f32->f64; `bool` correctly non-numeric; references excluded before the integer helpers strip them); ttEquals' field coverage per kind (TY_REF mut+nullable+inner, TY_ARRAY asize+inner, TY_PARAM tpIndex+name, TY_FN ret+params, TY_GENERIC mut+sdef+targs, TY_ENUM edef+targs, TY_DYN name) - the only kind that falls to the final `return false` is TY_STRUCT, which is safe because every TY_STRUCT node is the per-StructDef cache `sd->type` (types.c:213-217), and the hand-built struct types in check_expr.c:834 and check_top.c:3969 are never looked up by name; ttArray/ttGeneric/ttEnumGeneric/ttFn interning keys (sdef/edef + argument lists) match their equality predicates; the concreteness tests (ttHasParam over REF/ARRAY/FN/GENERIC/ENUM) do cover the constructors that can carry a parameter, so `ttGeneric`/`ttFn` keep provisional instances out of the tables (only `ttArray` interns unconditionally, and codegen filters those with `mentionsParam`, codegen.c:6797); ttViewMut/ttViewReadonly/ttSubstitute round-trip `mut` through substitution; the coroutine 2-parameter/1-argument fallback in ttSubstitute (types.c:827) is reachable only for `coroutine<T>` because every other arity mismatch is rejected in ttResolve (checked all `ttGeneric`/`ttEnumGeneric` callers and `funcInstance`, whose targs vector is always as long as the template's parameter list, with NULL slots rejected at check_expr.c:3160 and check_top.c:5008).

No size/alignment code exists in this unit: there is no `ttSize`/`ttAlign` in types.c or anywhere in src/ (grep), so the 'size and alignment' part of the brief has no code to review here; the only size-adjacent predicate is `ttIntBits`, whose table (8/16/32/64) and callers (check.c:344-354 literal range, codegen.c:2596-2613 float conversion) I checked for boundary handling.

Could not confirm / left unreported: (1) `ttViewMut` (types.c:749) assigns the base instance's `targs` Vec *header* to the shadow, so the two share one buffer; every consumer I found only reads it, so I could not build a failing program - it is a latent aliasing hazard, not a demonstrated defect. (2) The `ttCrossesC` check for a written `fn(...)` type is skipped while a signature mentions a type parameter (types.c:417) and the substituted signature is never re-checked, so `fn(slice<u8>) -> void` can be manufactured through a generic instantiation; the comment acknowledges the gap and I could not turn it into C that breaks (the generated typedef and both sides of the call agree), so I did not file it. (3) `ttEquals` would compare two TY_ENUM nodes with `edef == NULL` as equal, but no path in the compiler builds such a node (all TY_ENUM producers set edef), so it is not reachable. (4) `ttIsBuiltinName` (types.h:83, types.c:27) has no caller anywhere in the repository - dead but harmless. (5) A generic struct literal written with arguments (`box<i32> { ... }`) is a parse-level rejection; I did not investigate it as it is outside this unit. All repro files are under /tmp/tt/ and each finding's repro was run against ./build/extc (Sep 30 01:42).
